id: I'm a Fool to Love You

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Some folks will tell you the blues is a woman, Some type of supernatural creature. My mother would tell you, if she could, About her life with my father, A strange and sometimes cruel gentleman. She would tell you about the choices A young black woman faces. Is falling in love with some man A deal with the devil In blue terms, the tongue we use When we don't want nuance To get in the way, When we need to talk straight. My mother chooses my father After choosing a man Who was, as we sing it, Of no account. This man made my father look good, That's how bad it was. He made my father seem like an island In the middle of a stormy sea, He made my father look like a rock. And is the blues the moment you realize You exist in a stacked deck, You look in a mirror at your young face, The face my sister carries, And you know it's the only leverage You've got. Does this create a hurt that whispersHow you going to do? Is the blues the moment You shrug your shoulders And agree, a girl without money Is nothing, dust To be pushed around by any old breeze. Compared to this, My father seems, briefly, To be a fire escape. This is the way the blues works Its sorry wonders, Makes trouble look like A feather bed, Makes the wrong man's kisses A healing.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

This poem explores the blues as a metaphor for the difficult romantic and economic choices faced by a young Black woman—the speaker's mother—who selects the speaker's father not out of ideal love but as the lesser of harsh options. Through vivid imagery contrasting the father as a "rock" or "fire escape" against an even worse previous partner, the poem reveals how the blues transforms desperation and limited choices into something bearable, making "trouble look like a feather bed" and illuminating the painful compromises born of poverty and gender inequality.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Some, About, She

outputs.L1:
Some will tell you the blues is a woman,
some manner of supernatural creature.
My mother would tell you, if she could,
about her life with my father,
a strange and sometimes cruel gentleman.
She would tell you about the choices
a young Black woman faces—
whether falling in love with a man
is a bargain struck with the devil,
spoken in blue terms, the tongue we use
when we won't let nuance
stand in the way,
when we need to speak plainly.

My mother chooses my father
after choosing a man
who was, as we sing it,
of no account.
This man made my father look good—
that is how bad it was.
He made my father seem an island
adrift in a stormy sea,
he made my father look like a rock.

And is the blues the moment you realize
you exist within a stacked deck,
you gaze in the mirror at your young face,
the face my sister now carries,
and you know it is the only leverage
you possess?
Does this give rise to a hurt that whispers,
How are you going to manage?

Is the blues the moment
you shrug your shoulders
and concede that a girl without money
is nothing, mere dust
pushed about by any passing breeze?
Compared to this,
my father seems, for a moment,
a fire escape.

This is how the blues works
its sorry wonders,
makes trouble look like
a feather bed,
makes the wrong man's kisses
a kind of healing.
outputs.L2:
There are people who claim the blues takes the form of a woman, some kind of otherworldly being. My mother, if she were able, would speak to you about her years spent with my father—an odd man who could be harsh at times. She would explain the decisions that confront a young Black woman. Is giving your heart to a man like striking a bargain with the devil? I put it in blues language, the plain speech we reach for when we want to strip away complexity and simply say things directly.

My mother settled on my father only after she'd been with another man—one who, to borrow the phrase from our songs, amounted to nothing. Beside that man, my father appeared respectable; that's the depth of how awful it was. Next to him, my father seemed like solid ground in the midst of a raging ocean, steady as stone.

And maybe the blues is that instant when it dawns on you that the odds are rigged against you. You gaze into a mirror at your youthful reflection—the very features my sister now bears—and you understand that your looks are the sole bargaining chip you possess. Doesn't this plant a pain that murmurs, What are you going to do?

Is the blues that instant when you lift your shoulders in surrender and admit that a penniless girl counts for nothing, mere dust shoved around by whatever wind blows through? Against a truth like that, my father momentarily resembles an escape route to safety.

This is how the blues performs its miserable magic—it dresses up hardship to look like a soft place to rest, and turns the kisses of the wrong man into something that seems to heal.
outputs.L3:
# Understanding the Blues Through Lived Experience

The poem explores the blues not as a mythical creature or abstract musical tradition, but as a lens for understanding the harsh realities of a young Black woman's life. Rather than romanticizing sorrow, the poem uses the blues as a framework for examining the concrete circumstances that shape a woman's choices and self-perception. In this way, the blues becomes a way of seeing and interpreting the world—one born from struggle and hardship.

At the heart of the poem is the speaker's mother, who faced difficult choices about love and survival. Hers was not a story of romantic idealism but of practical calculation under impossible conditions. Ultimately, she selected the speaker's father over an even worse partner, making a decision that reflects the limited and painful options available to her. This choice reveals how love, for many women in her position, was intertwined with the basic need to survive.

The blues, then, represents the painful moment of realizing you are trapped in an unfair system—one where your youth and beauty are your only leverage. This awareness is devastating precisely because it acknowledges how few resources a young woman possesses when navigating a world stacked against her. Her value is measured by fleeting physical qualities, and the recognition of this reality is itself a kind of blues.

Compounding this entrapment is the crushing weight of poverty, which forces the mother to see herself as worthless and powerless. She comes to view herself as "dust to be pushed around by any old breeze," an image that captures her sense of insignificance and lack of control over her own fate. Under such conditions, even a flawed man could seem like an escape—a way out of destitution and vulnerability, however imperfect that refuge might be.

Finally, the blues distorts perception itself, making suffering appear comforting and transforming the wrong man's affection into something that feels like healing. This distortion is perhaps the most tragic dimension of the poem: the way hardship can warp one's judgment until pain masquerades as solace and a damaging relationship feels like salvation. In illuminating this psychological reality, the poem reveals the blues not merely as sadness, but as a profound and complicated way of enduring an unjust world.
outputs.L4:
# The Blues as Survival: Love and Choice in Hard Times

The poem takes the blues—that distinctly American musical tradition born from Black suffering and endurance—and transforms it into a lens through which we witness one woman's constrained romantic decisions. At its heart is the speaker's mother, a young Black woman navigating a world where love is rarely a matter of pure desire or ideal partnership. Instead, her choices are shaped and limited by the intersecting pressures of poverty and gender inequality, forces that narrow her options until choosing a partner becomes less about romance than about survival.

The central revelation of the poem is that the mother did not select the speaker's father out of soaring passion or storybook love. Rather, she chose him as the lesser of harsh options—a pragmatic decision made by someone who understood that the alternatives were worse. This is not a story of romance triumphing over circumstance, but of a woman making the most sensible choice available in a situation that offered few good ones.

The poem renders this dynamic vivid through its imagery. The father is described as a "rock" or a "fire escape"—metaphors that reveal much about his role in the mother's life. He is not portrayed as an object of desire but as something solid to cling to, a means of escape from danger, a source of stability in an unstable world. These are images of refuge rather than passion, of practical salvation rather than emotional fulfillment. Crucially, this relatively favorable portrait emerges only in contrast to an even worse previous partner, against whom the father appears as a genuine improvement. The mother's choice, then, is defined not by the father's virtues alone but by how much better he seemed compared to what came before.

It is here that the blues performs its essential work. The poem suggests that this musical form has the power to transform desperation and limited choices into something bearable—to take the raw material of hardship and render it survivable. In one of the poem's most striking phrases, the blues makes "trouble look like a feather bed," softening suffering enough that a person can rest upon it. The blues does not erase pain or resolve injustice; instead, it provides a way of enduring them, a means of finding beauty and comfort within circumstances that might otherwise be unbearable.

Ultimately, the poem illuminates the painful compromises that arise from poverty and gender inequality. The mother's decision stands as a testament to the constrained agency of Black women whose romantic and economic lives were bound together, whose choices about love could not be separated from questions of safety, shelter, and survival. Through the blues, the poem honors these difficult negotiations, refusing to romanticize them while also recognizing the resilience and quiet strength required to make them. In doing so, it transforms one woman's story into a broader meditation on how people endure, and even find a kind of grace, amid limited and painful choices.
outputs.L5:
# She

She moved through the world with a quiet confidence that drew people in. There was something about the way she carried herself—unhurried, thoughtful, present in each moment.

Some people spend their whole lives searching for who they are. Not her. She had found her center long ago, in the small things: the first cup of coffee at dawn, the pages of a well-worn book, the laughter shared with old friends.

There was a story behind every choice she made. Some of those stories she kept close, tucked away like pressed flowers between the pages of memory. Others she shared freely, her voice bright with the joy of the telling.

People often wondered about her—about where she came from, about the dreams that lit her eyes when she spoke of the future. She was, in many ways, a mystery, but not the kind that frustrates. Rather, she was the kind of mystery that invites you to lean closer, to listen a little more carefully.

Some days were harder than others. She knew this, accepted it. On those days, she was gentle with herself, understanding that even the strongest among us need rest. And when the sun rose again, she rose with it, ready to face whatever came.

That was the thing about her. No matter what life brought, she met it with grace. And in doing so, she taught everyone around her something about resilience, about hope, about the quiet power of simply being yourself.

Some people leave footprints. She left something more—a feeling, a warmth, a reminder that the world is a little brighter with people like her in it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about the blues as a way of understanding a mother's difficult choices in love, told from the perspective of her child.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Blues Taught Me

My mother played Billie Holiday
on Sunday mornings
when the men were gone
and the house exhaled.

I was too young to know
that "Good Morning Heartache"
was not a song
but a confession.

She'd stir the grits slow,
hips swaying to a grief
I couldn't name,
and I thought that's what love was—

a woman moving
to music that hurt her,
choosing again and again
the note that bent blue.

Now I understand:
she stayed for the ones who stayed,
left the ones who left first,
and some she loved

the way you love a storm
from a doorway—
close enough to feel it,
far enough to survive.

I judged her once.
The revolving door of fathers,
the phone calls at midnight,
the way she'd disappear

into a man's rough voice
like it was a country
she'd been trying to reach
her whole life.

But the blues don't apologize.
They just tell you
what happened,
how it felt,

and trust you'll grow
into the understanding.
I'm grown now.
I know the difference

between a song about pain
and the pain itself—
how my mother lived
in the space between,

making something almost like beauty
out of every hard thing
she was handed,
humming through it,

teaching me without words
that survival, sometimes,
is its own
kind of love song.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem exploring how poverty limits the choices available to a young black woman, using the blues as a central metaphor.
counterfactuals.output:
# Blues in a Minor Key

She wakes to morning like a borrowed song,
the melody already written down—
each note a door somebody bolted shut
before her mama came to this hard town.

The blues know how to bend a single line,
to take one grief and turn it seven ways;
but bending isn't choosing where to go,
it's only how you survive the narrow days.

*I could have been*, she hums above the sink,
*a doctor, teacher, anything at all*—
but tuition is a chord she cannot reach,
her fingers stretching, stretching, still too small.

The landlord plays his rent like a refrain,
the same twelve bars come circling every month.
She works two jobs to keep the rhythm steady,
too tired to dream, too proud to want for lunch.

They say the blues is freedom—so it seems—
the freedom of the caged bird's practiced trill,
who makes the bars themselves into a music,
who sings because she cannot cross the sill.

And oh, she's got a voice could fill a hall,
could rise like smoke above the tired street—
but no one hands a scholarship to sound,
and genius starves without enough to eat.

So this is how the melody stays low:
not that she lacks the range to reach the high,
but every high note costs what she can't spend,
and so she holds the ground note, and gets by.

Yet listen—when she sings, the whole room stills.
There's power in the way she works the pain,
transforms the little given into gold,
makes beauty from the shackle and the chain.

The blues won't lie and call her struggle just.
It names the theft, it testifies the wrong.
But in her throat, the sorrow turns to fire—
she's more than what they left her. She's the song.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Cornelius Eady that reflects on a mother choosing between two flawed men and what the blues teaches us about desperation.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Blues Knows**

My mother had two men to choose from
and the blues to help her choose.

One could hold a note
but not a job.
One could hold a job
but not his tongue,
and both of them
knew how to leave a room
the way weather leaves,
sudden, then all over you.

Understand:
this is not a story
about love.
This is a story
about arithmetic,
about a woman doing sums
at a kitchen table
while the radio
taught her the difference
between wanting
and needing to stay alive.

The blues never lies
to a woman like that.
It doesn't say *he'll change.*
It says *he won't,
now what.*
It says *desperation
is just hunger
that has learned to sing,*
and my mother
had a good ear,
God help her,
a good ear.

So she picked the one
whose flaws
she could see coming,
the way you pick
the storm you know
over the storm
you'd have to learn.

And the record spun
its patient lesson:
that choosing
is a kind of grief,
that the woman who chooses
is not saved,
only certain—
and certainty,
the blues will tell you,
is the last thing
we can afford
and the only thing
we buy.

I was not born yet.
I am the interest
on that decision,
the small change
left on the table
after everybody paid.
And when I hear
that music now
I understand
my mother
did not fall in love.

She did the math.
She heard the man
inside the song
say *baby, baby,*
and she knew
that *baby*
was a word
two desperate people
use
to keep from
saying
*help.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a narrative poem where the speaker reflects on their parents' relationship, describing the father as barely better than a worse alternative.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Lesser Weather**

My mother married rain when she was young—
that's how she told it, later, at the sink,
her hands gone soft in dishwater and thought.
She'd wanted sun. She got a colder thing.

But rain, she said, is better than the drought.
She'd known men who were fire and men who fled,
and Father, though he never learned to speak
the language that a woman wants in bed

or kitchen, coat, or long uncertain year,
at least came home. He came home every night.
He set his boots beside the door, took off
the day, and slept. He wasn't wrong. Not right,

exactly, either. Somewhere in between,
a man who paid the mortgage, mowed the yard,
and once, when I was nine and split my chin,
drove ninety through the dark, his knuckles hard

and pale around the wheel, and said my name
just once, the way you'd say a word you fear
to overuse in case it wears too thin.
That was the closest love I saw him near.

My mother measured him in what he wasn't:
not cruel, not gone, not drinking through the rent.
The bar was on the floor. He cleared it, barely.
She loved the inches of his slow ascent.

And I have spent my life inside that arithmetic—
the grateful math of *could have been much worse*—
learning that a man can be a shelter
and still let all the warmth out through the doors.

I don't forgive him. I don't quite condemn.
He was the lesser weather, gray and low,
a roof that kept the harder storm from us
by being, every day, the storm we'd know.

And when he died, my mother didn't weep
so much as settle, like a house at rest
when someone finally leaves and lets it breathe.
*He wasn't much,* she said. *But he was best*

*of what I thought I'd get.* And that's the grief—
not that he failed us, but that he was chosen
against a darker backdrop, and so passed,
and so was mourned, half-thawed and mostly frozen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that defines what the blues is through a series of questions, connecting it to family history, hard choices, and making the wrong love feel like comfort.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Blues Is

Is it the sound my grandmother swallowed
while ironing other people's linen,
the hum she kept behind her teeth
like a coin saved for hard weather?

Is it the road my father didn't take,
or the one he did—the north-bound bus,
the door he closed so soft
it never made a sound to wake us?

What do you call the ache
that arrives dressed like a friend,
that sits at your table and eats your bread
and you set a place for it again?

Is it the choosing wrong
because wrong knows your name,
because the hand that hurts you
is the only hand that stayed?

Is it my mother saying *stay*
to a man who wouldn't,
her voice a rope she threw across the dark
and hauled back empty?

Tell me—
is the blues the wound
or the way we learn to wear it,
the shape our sorrow takes
when it decides to sing?

Is it comfort dressed as ruin,
ruin dressed as home,
the familiar cold of a bed
we make ourselves, alone?

Or is it this:
the question passed down
like a color in the blood—
how we keep asking
what hurts us,
and calling it love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
